scenes.narration: You've accumulated years of experience.
Projects delivered, teams supported, and stakeholders managed. But your next step probably feels less clear than your first job did.
Here's the thing: not all transitions are the same, and the advice that fits one can sink another. Almost any career change sorts along two questions.

vars.statement: Almost Any Change Sorts Along Two Questions

scenes.narration: First—did you choose it, or did it choose you? That's the difference between a chosen move and a forced one.

vars.label: Question one
vars.heading: Did You Choose It, or Did It Choose You?

scenes.narration: Second—how big is the leap? Are you building on your past in an adjacent direction, or reinventing into something genuinely new?
Cross those two questions, and you get four kinds of career transition.

vars.context: Cross those two questions and you get four kinds of career transition

scenes.narration: The first is the Pivot—a change you chose that still builds on your past. You're moving to adjacent territory. Same core strengths, new context.

vars.heading: The Pivot: Chosen and Adjacent
vars.chips: A change you chose,Adjacent territory,New context

scenes.narration: Think finance to product, or teaching to instructional design. Because your experience carries forward, a pivot is lower-risk and faster than it looks.

vars.label: In practice
vars.heading: What a Pivot Looks Like
vars.chips: Finance to product,Teaching to instructional design

scenes.narration: Your job is less to prove brand-new skills than to reframe the ones you already have.
The second is the Reinvention—also a change you chose, but this time into something genuinely new.

vars.heading: The Reinvention: Chosen and New
vars.chips: A change you chose,Genuinely new territory

scenes.narration: You're deliberately changing fields, and often changing part of your identity along with it. Think of an editor who becomes a fashion designer.
The upside is real, but so is the cost: reinvention asks for more identity work and more experimentation before it clicks.

vars.lines: More identity work|More experimentation before it clicks

scenes.narration: The third is the Rebuild—a change you did not choose, but one that keeps you near your field.

vars.heading: The Rebuild: Not Chosen, Still Adjacent
vars.chips: Not something you chose,Still near your field

scenes.narration: A layoff or a life event pushed you, yet the work you're heading toward still builds on what you already know.

pointCues: a layoff or a life event
still builds on what you already know

vars.label: The rebuild
vars.heading: Pushed by Circumstance
vars.point1: A layoff or a life event
vars.point2: The work still builds on what you know

scenes.narration: The practical path here is usually shorter than it feels. The harder part is emotional, because you didn't ask for it.

pointCues: because you didn't ask for it

vars.lines: Shorter than it feels|Hard, because you did not ask for it

scenes.narration: Your first job is to process that loss so it doesn't quietly leak into your interviews.
The fourth is the Forced Reinvention—the hardest of the four. Here you were pushed out and the old path is closed, so you're reinventing into something new without having chosen to.

vars.heading: The Forced Reinvention: Not Chosen and New

scenes.narration: It asks the most of you: extra care, extra support, and extra experimentation while you find your footing.

vars.label: What it takes
vars.heading: What Forced Reinvention Asks of You

scenes.narration: But it's also where some of the most remarkable reinventions come from—when necessity clears away the "shoulds," people often build something they would never have reached for on their own.
None of these four is "better" than the others. Knowing which one you're in tells you what to plan for.

vars.statement: None of These Four Is Better

scenes.narration: How much identity work and grief to expect, and how much experimenting you'll need before you commit.

vars.label: What to expect
vars.heading: How Much to Expect
vars.point1: Identity work and grief to expect

scenes.narration: So whenever your next move feels foggy, ask the two questions: Did I choose this, or did it choose me? And how big is the leap?
In this module, you'll reflect on your current role, your desired role, and what success would look like over the next year.

vars.label: In this module
vars.heading: Reflect on Where You Are
vars.point3: What success looks like next year

scenes.narration: Then you'll use an AI activity to analyze the projects that energize you. So your choice is grounded in evidence, not just impulse.

vars.statement: An AI Activity Analyzes What Energizes You

scenes.narration: Finally, you'll capture your direction in a simple Next Move Statement for the next 6–12 months.
You don't need to solve your entire career here. You only need to recognize which of these four transitions you're in right now.
That clarity is what creates momentum.
